analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to sign away their right to sue over job disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would void mandatory arbitration agreements covering workplace disputes, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended on Jan. 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers commonly require workers, as a condition of getting a job, to agree that any dispute — unpaid wages, discrimination, harassment, firing — will be decided by a private arbitrator rather than a judge or jury, and to give up the right to join a class action. This bill would make those agreements unenforceable. It would also make post-dispute arbitration agreements valid only if the worker chose them freely: with a plain-language explanation, a 45-day waiting period, written consent, and a guarantee of no retaliation for refusing. It covers employees and independent contractors alike, and it would leave union contracts (which have their own negotiated grievance systems) untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers: anyone whose employer made them sign an arbitration agreement at hiring — which covers most large private-sector employers' workforces. It protects employees and independent contractors regardless of how the employer labels them, and it gives workers who face retaliation for refusing to arbitrate a right to sue with attorney's fees paid.

how_it_helps.text: Makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements covering work disputes — including waivers of class or collective claims — void and unenforceable, so workers keep access to court and juries.

Allows arbitration only after a dispute arises, and only if the agreement is not coerced, is explained in plain language, follows a 45-day waiting period, and is signed with written affirmative consent; the deadline for filing claims is paused during that waiting period.

Prohibits employers from retaliating against or threatening any worker who refuses to agree to arbitration, and gives the worker a right to sue within two years (three for willful violations), with attorney's fees and costs.

Amends the National Labor Relations Act so that agreements barring employees from pursuing joint, class, or collective claims are an unfair labor practice and void, extending federal labor-law protection to that concerted activity.

Applies to employees and to independent contractors regardless of how the employer classifies them, closes a common evasion route, and leaves arbitration in union collective bargaining agreements in place.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially large companies that use arbitration agreements to keep workplace claims out of court and out of class actions — would face more lawsuits and higher litigation exposure. Arbitration providers would lose a large stream of employment business. Some businesses argue these costs could be passed on in slower hiring or lower pay.

drawbacks.text: Employers and arbitration's defenders argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for individual workers than court litigation, and that removing it raises costs; the bill responds by preserving individual claims but restoring the class-action deterrent that individual arbitration cases cannot provide.

The bill sets strict conditions even for post-dispute arbitration agreements (45-day waiting period, written disclosure, affirmative written consent), so an employer and a worker who genuinely want to settle a dispute by arbitration must clear procedural hurdles that could make arbitration unusable even when both sides prefer it.

It takes effect immediately and applies to any dispute arising after enactment even if the worker already signed an arbitration agreement, so companies would face sudden changes to signed contracts and new litigation exposure without a phase-in.
It applies broadly to any 'covered entity' engaging a worker, including small businesses, which would face the same bar on arbitration agreements as large corporations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: an arbitration agreement signed at hiring means a fired or underpaid worker typically argues alone before a private decision-maker whose rulings are hard to appeal, and class actions — often the only economical way to challenge small-dollar wage theft — are barred. The costs fall on employers in litigation exposure and on anyone who genuinely preferred a quick arbitration, for whom the bill's voluntary-agreement conditions add friction. The bill leaves union grievance systems intact, which limits the disruption where workers already have a negotiated alternative.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2024 and referred to the House Judiciary and Education and Workforce Committees, neither of which ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, joined by Rep. Robert Scott of Virginia, introduced the bill on June 11, 2024, in the final months of the 118th Congress.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Education and Workforce Committee, for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.
No further action is recorded: the bill received no committee markup, no hearing result, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It had 10 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support was recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on forced arbitration keep the status quo: workers remain bound to individual arbitration and barred from class actions, with no court access restored.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought House action; it was assigned to two committees with jurisdiction over labor and arbitration law.

for.name: Rep. Robert C. Scott

for.what_they_did: Added their names in support of the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary and Education and Workforce Committees
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred (Republican majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the June 2024 referral — no markup, no hearing result, no committee vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Employer and business trade groups
against.role: Opposition to bans on forced arbitration of workplace disputes
against.what_they_did: Long-running public campaigns by employer groups against congressional bans on mandatory arbitration agreements, which are treated by large employers as protection from class-action litigation over wages, discrimination, and harassment.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority the bill never advanced past referral; no Republican cosponsor is recorded.

industries.industry: Employers using arbitration agreements (especially large corporations)
industries.note: The bill voids the agreements these companies use to keep wage, discrimination, and harassment claims out of court and out of class actions, exposing them to jury trials and collective suits. Mandatory individual arbitration is widely documented as producing lower worker recovery rates, so the industry's interest here runs against workers' access to remedies.
Private arbitration firms would lose a major stream of employment disputes, which the bill removes from their mandatory pipeline except for tightly conditioned post-dispute agreements.

Union contracts are expressly carved out and the NLRA amendment protects concerted, joint claims — the kind of collective action unions organize. Arbitration in a collectively bargained agreement remains valid.
Restored court access plus fee-shifting for retaliation claims means more viable cases for plaintiffs' employment lawyers, whose incentives track workers' ability to sue.
